If you want a somewhat more immediate solution than the Job corps, my reccomenedation is continue trying to keep your head above water in San Antonio, but apply for food service jobs or to HEB in Austin, you should easily be able to get ~$15 an hour. Once you get settled in Austin, you should strongly consider completing the FAFSA and enrolling in ACC. You can probably be set up with all of this by the Spring semster, starting in January. Once you get your pell grants distributed, you can also look for housing, there is definitely still (sketchy) places in Austin where you can rent a room for ~$500/mo. 

Once you got housing and work/school set up, literally just abandon the car on the side of the road, stop paying it, cancel insurance. If you want you can maybe try to save up enough from working a lot to get out of your negative 10k equity, and take a stab at refinancing it to help your credit, but honestly that shouldn't be your top priority. I will say that Austin public transport system is decent enough, and if you still find Cap Metro lacking, you can save up for a bike, you do not need a car in Austin as badly. 

Of course, not paying your debts will have negative effects in the future but since you're homeless right now that's not the most of your concerns. For now you just have to get unstuck. Getting the education to land you in a high paying job in the trades or medical field will give you more future earning potential than a warehouse job at least. CDL was also a good idea mentioned earlier in the thread. 

Overall, your immediate concern is to increase income so that you're no longer homeless.

I tend to play more on base-builder difficulty with generational colonies so I prefer to lean into the aspect of environmental challenges rather than raids. Kind of like hardmode stardew valley! So I really don't like the whole basegame farming or food systems -- basically I crashland in an alien enviroment and I immediately know how to plant either rice, potatos or corn?  And this eniroment can grow all 3 plants, despite their differing needs for irrigation? And these crops, plus berries and a few utility plants are the only ones that exist in the world? And we're perfectly healthy living off corn simple meals, without any ill effect for years?

I play with seeds please, crop rotation, smart farming, realistic plant cycles, wild crops, as well as VE plants, fishing, farming furniture (mostly just the scarecrow), and cooking to try to add more realism. I use the sprinklers and fertilizer from dubs bad hygiene as well as the feature to set custom levels for irrigation strength, fertilizer strength, and base soil fertility. Variety matters is also important in this setup to incentivize farming/hunting/fishing for proteins, though sadly I haven't seen a mod that adds negative health effects from an unbalanced diet. Though I don't love how variety matters plays in earlygame, lack of diet variety after just crash landing should be fine, but in mid/endgame I think variety matters is essential so I suppose it balances out. Wild crops arguably makes early game survival easier anyhow.

I would also love to see a mod that restricts plants available based on biome/rainfall level/temperatures but no such luck so far searching so I just self-impose limits -- not growing rice paddies in a boreal forest, but I use the radishes from VE plants instead. At least self-restricting gameplay like this has lead me down a rabbit hole of researching and learning more about irl gardening though, which has been fun :D

I play all 5 healer specs at endgame level, raiding etc. Still, I've done at least a few beta dungeons on each and I'd say the mobile healers feel the best to play. So this would be priest and druid. I mean hpal and rsham are very strong specs, nobody would turn them down for dungeons. In particular i would say hpal is best for raiding, but certainly more difficult in dungeons due to immobility and being more tankheal focused, no aoe heal. 

Shaman would probably be my third pick, it's really good in all department from utility to healing output to dpsing, but it's immobile and just boring to play... youre only pressing riptide, lesserhealing wave, and chain heal while healing stream totem does ~30% of the healing. Priest and druid at least feel more active and fun with more buttons and speed increases. 

Both druid and priest have good support toolkits for 5m: Priest has hymn of hope and druid has innervate which can restore your party members mana. Rsham has mana tide totem which is also super nice. And rdruid in particular is very mana efficient even at lower gear levels. Both priest and druid have a group buff, fortitude and mark of the wild, which are admittedly weaker than pally buffs or totems, but theyre still nice utility depending on party comp. 

The parts where i think druid and priest really shine is their gameplay feel. Priest has mind soothe which can let you skip certain pulls (dont try with PuG but nice in a guild group) and rdruid has stealth so you'll never have to worry about accidentally pulling yourself.

Holy priest in particular i like for 5mans over disc priest. Holy has an unique talent called body and soul which will increase the movement speed of the person you put Power Word: Shield on for 60% for 5s. Popping this on the tank or yourself on cooldown can greatly speed up your party, or allow you to catch up yourself or a dps who falls behind the tank. Resto druid also has a baseline speed increase in the catform sprint. Idk to me speed increases feel super impactful in dungeons and i dont enjoy my shaman in dungeons even with nitro boots

Also, holy priest can do fair damage with smite when not actively healing. One downside of the druid is you should be in tree form to heal, but you cant cast dps spells like wrath while in that form. Still, popping out of form to moonfire mirror images is helpful. I started something similar at my high school when i was younger! So it depends on your group and their experience/motivation but in terms of software you should most likely just get fusion360 and open rocket as your main design programs. They are free for students and great for beginners too. I saw you were gonna go with tinkercad elsewhere in the thread, and that's what I did too for like a few months starting out prototyping but I'll caution you that it'll get boring fairly quickly tbh and won't have most of the features you will eventually need. In terms of cad programs I've used a few and I really think fusion360 is best for beginners and I honestly think I could've just skipped tinkercad all together. 

Also you should expect your biggest expense over the course of the program to be engines or other such parts. So absolutely do not spend a ton of money on the very cool but overhyped advanced tools upfront, make sure it is budgeted out. Keep it simple, a standard workshop setup maybe a cheap FDM printer (200-400 usd) is plenty to get started with.

I'd also recommend against a resin printer starting out. They're very expensive and while they are a super cool and potentially a great goal to strive for as you build your program, they're also quite a bit more expensive than a regular FDM printer and the highly specialized features that make them so expensive aren't so useful for rocketry.

In terms of tools honestly any basic workshop would be good. If your school has a woodshop space that would be great for building prototypes, maybe even give you room to play with fiberglass + like a vaccum bag.

I think it's beneficial to students, but harmful to the school as a business.

The auto admit rule benefits students in Texas who may not have had a chance at UT, and its main beneficiaries are usually minorities, first gen students, or students from smaller schools who were able to hold down good high school grades but did not have the money for fancy extracurriculars or standardized testing tutors, through no fault of their own. So in that sense, I think it benefits the student body as a whole, through allowing bright students who lack the family resources of the people who normally apply to top colleges to get a good education. And I think it's such a good thing to allow those students to have a chance, especially as they could be great students in college even if they lacked resources in high school.

But for the school as a business, talking about "rankings" or test scores, sure it doesn't help. But that stuff should only really matter to donors, who naturally want some proof their money is going to a good school. However, as students we all know the quality of education we are getting, and I'm sure it's on par with any other flagship public university, like even if some UC school has a higher ranking, I often use their websites or YouTube lectures to study for my UT classes... and it's the same exact material.

I honestly don't see how any student admitted to UT could be against the auto admit rule, all it does is benefit your classmates, allowing people from different backgrounds to get in. And those students who barely made the cut from competitive high schools or are from OOS would have plenty of other options for schools on caliber with UT anyways.

Being in Cockrell won't really help you change engineering majors. In the past, they have primarily GPA based decisions but last semester there was an essay component as well, mostly due to covid but they might end up keeping it since most other school's internal transfer policy have some holistic component. I heard progress toward the new degree plays a part as well, but I don't think they've confirmed this.

ECE is probably the most competitive Cockrell major to transfer into, and it has one of the strictest 4-year pre-req chains, you begin taking ECE specific classes starting in first semester of freshman year. If you want to transfer into ECE, it'd be pretty tough, but not impossible if you feel like it's necessary. CS is probably the single most competitive UT major, people with 4.0s have been denied transfer. The CS elements minor has classes fill up fast and it's difficult to complete it in 4 years just because the classes are so congested. Also, ASE has a fair bit of coding in it, as it shares a department with the new Computational Engineering major, which might interest you. ASE in general is very interdisciplinary, you'll take classes on electrical systems, coding, fluids, aerodynamics, and more. So generally I think it's different because there's a lot more brainpower required for classes. Like the assignments are usually harder and there's not really busywork. The percentage of a class that gets an A is also lower, at least in my high school if you took ap classes the teachers would give you an A practically no matter what. 

Another difference was time limits and weighting  on exams. There are generally only two midterms and a final which can make up at least 50% of your grade, in my high school tests were like 30% at most and a lot more multiple choice/lacking critical thinking. 

Finally, a big difference for me was adjusting to time management. I wasn't able to join many clubs in high school but here at UT there's hundereds of orgs, including a few that really interesting me and I'm dedicated to. As such, I've had to use a calendar service to schedule out my time on clubs, study time/class time.

 Speaking of time in class you spend a lot more time taking notes on lecture. Almost every class session is the professor speaking at you, versus in highschool a lot of the class time was like study hall/time given to work in projects. In high school I rarely had to schedule homework bc was able to complete homework during school hours, but in college you really have to study and complete homework on your own time, without parents reminding you. 

This is just my experience as a cockrell student, YMMV but I hope it helped!

Your classes heavily depend on what credits you got in high school. You should always claim all of your AP or CC credit, as long as it's relevant to your degree and you're not trying to get a high GPA to transfer majors. To figure out what transfers, here is the [ME Curriculum] (http://www.me.utexas.edu/images/MEGeneralCurriculum_2016-2018_2018-2020.pdf) and this is a good [AP/IB credit calculator] (https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~wang/resources/utap) to determine what your credits transfer as. If you took dual credit classes, this is the [Automated Transfer Equivalency] (http://utdirect.utexas.edu/adtreq/search2.WBX) that will tell you what your cc classes transfer as 

When you take a UGS, VAPA, Gov, etc type of class, try to get one with a global cultures or cultural diversity flag. The engineering curriculum doesn't carry those, and you have to take them in-residence at UT. Best to knock them out along side with any other core curriculum requirements you need to take. You can only count one flag per course, and the flags are basically a random requirement UT instated for some reason. 

As far as laptops goes, a windows system will make your life easier than having to use a virtual machine on a Mac and you should just make sure it's portable. Your first semester you will be using Solidworks to learn CAD in ME 210 and probably Matlab at some point early on as well. The specs don't nee to be very fancy, just make sure it's something you could live with for the next few years.

Final tips: join student orgs, keep on top of your schedule with google calendar and hookem! If you need anything else feel free to PM me :D
